THE_LAW: Nothing reaches a slide that is not in this file. Every number rides with 'per the owner, on his own podcast' or its stated label, in the same breath. There is ZERO independent corroboration for this case.

case.company: The Wilson Companies (operating as Wilson Plumbing, Heating, Cooling and Electric Inc.)
case.legal_name: Wilson Plumbing, Heating, Cooling and Electric Inc.
case.ownership: Family owned, third generation, CEO John Wilson
case.size: over 200 employees (self-reported in John Wilson's own bio; NOT independently corroborated)
case.industry: Residential and commercial home services: plumbing, HVAC, electrical
case.capability: Voice AI that answers inbound calls, books the job into ServiceTitan, detects a frustrated caller and hands off to a human CSR, plus a separate product that scores calls for coaching
case.ladder_rung: 4 (workflow with a model in it, real tool use, designed human handoff)
case.ladder_justification: Steps are fixed and designed at build time, not chosen at run time. Onboarding starts from pre-built templates chosen by business size and service type, plus a job-type mapping and a customer-filled knowledge base. Bounded wired-in tool use into ONE system of record (ServiceTitan). Failure behaviour is to stop at a checkpoint and hand to a person, not to try another approach. Decisively, the vendor's own co-founder recommends the human-in-the-loop hybrid over full autonomy because the hybrid books better. That is a rung 4 answer to every question in the AGENTIC_LITERACY field guide. It is a good rung 4, not a rung 5.
case.vendor_label_used: Avoca describes itself as 'The AI Front Office for Service Businesses' with 'Always-on agents that answer every call', markets an 'AI CSR', and its site footer reads 'The AI workforce for service businesses'. The correction must be GENEROUS, not a dunk: this is a configured workflow with tool use and a human handoff, it is the right product for this job, and the vendor's own co-founder is on record that the version with the human in it books better.

bottleneck.text: The phones after hours. Wilson ran a 24/7 call centre and paid an outside answering service 8,000 dollars a month on top of it, and the outside service got worse after an acquisition.

claims.text: Wilson Plumbing, Heating, Cooling and Electric was started in 1958 by Ralph and Theresa Wilson in Akron, Ohio, and is family owned with the third generation of Wilsons involved.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "Ralph and Theresa Wilson started Wilson Plumbing & Heating in 1958" / "Now, 60 years later, we have the third generation of Wilsons involved with Paul's son, John Wilson." / "A Family-Owned & Operated HVAC Plumbing Provider" / "Serving Northeast Ohio"
claims.who_measured: The company, on its own About Us page
claims.date: Fetched 2026-08-15; page undated, '60 years later' phrasing implies copy written around 2018
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: per the company's own site
claims.notes: SINGLE RENDERING ONLY. Do NOT put '60 years' on a slide as a current figure, the About Us copy is stale. Say 'founded 1958', which is the durable fact.

claims.text: John Wilson is CEO of The Wilson Companies, an Ohio home services group he has grown from 3 million to over 40 million dollars in revenue, with over 200 employees.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "John Wilson is the CEO of The Wilson Companies" / "he's grown the family business from $3 million to over $40 million in revenue" / "has over 200 employees and more than $10M in EBITDA" / "an Ohio-based home services group"
claims.denominator: Whole company, all brands and locations, NOT the Akron plumbing entity alone
claims.who_measured: John Wilson, in his own biography on the website of the podcast he co-hosts
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: by his own account
claims.notes: CONFIRMED IN TWO INDEPENDENT RENDERINGS. This is the ONLY page proving qualifying filter 1 (50 to 1,000 employees), and it is a self-authored bio. Say '200-plus people', never a precise count. SCOPE MISMATCH: the 200-plus and the 40 million describe the GROUP across multiple locations and states. Do NOT imply all 200 work in Akron.

claims.text: Before Avoca, Wilson was paying 8,000 dollars a month to an outside answering service.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "we went from $8,000 a month to our answering service to, I honestly don't actually know what Evoke could cost, but I remember what 8,000 a month was."
claims.baseline: 8,000 dollars per month, the before figure
claims.denominator: Per month, for the outside answering service ONLY. Does NOT include the internal 24/7 call centre, a separate and larger cost.
claims.who_measured: John Wilson, the man who paid the invoice
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: the owner's own figure, said on his own podcast
claims.notes: CONFIRMED IN TWO INDEPENDENT RENDERINGS, digits identical. THE STRONGEST NUMBER IN THE CASE. Unhedged, specific, first person, a bill the speaker personally paid. 'Evoke' is machine-transcript garbling of 'Avoca'. This is the clean before-number and it carries the cost gate.

claims.text: Wilson said he does not actually know what Avoca costs him, but that it is definitely less than half of the 8,000 dollars a month he was paying the answering service, and put the figure at around 3,500 dollars a month.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "I honestly don't actually know what Evoke could cost, but I remember what 8,000 a month was. Yeah, definitely less than half of that. Yeah, sure. And it's around like th 3,500 or so." followed by "Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That, that rings a bell."
claims.baseline: The 8,000 dollars a month answering service it replaced
claims.denominator: Per month, LICENCE LAYER ONLY. Excludes integration, the call centre manager's configuration time, and change cost.
claims.who_measured: Nobody measured it. The CEO is approximating his own vendor bill and explicitly says so.
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: the owner's own ballpark, and he said out loud he did not know the exact number
claims.notes: EXPLICIT RULING ON THE COST GATE. THE GATE SURVIVES, but only in BOUNDED form. This is not a naked guess, it is a guess with a HARD UPPER BOUND from the man who signs the cheques. 'Definitely less than half of that' against a firmly remembered 8,000 is an order of magnitude with a ceiling, which ECONOMICS.md says satisfies the gate. A bare '3,500 dollars a month' on a slide is NOT honest and MUST NEVER APPEAR. Second problem: the transcript does not mark speaker turns inside this block, and the interleaved 'Yeah, sure' and 'That, that rings a bell' suggest the 3,500 may have been supplied by the Avoca guest and merely agreed to by Wilson. THE SPEAKER OF THE DIGITS IS UNCERTAIN. SHIP AS: 'less than half of the 8,000 dollar answering service it replaced, which the owner ballparked at around 3,500 a month while saying he did not actually know the figure.' THE BOUND IS THE CLAIM. The 3,500 is colour.

claims.text: Wilson's call centre went from 18 CSRs to 10, and he attributes that to a mix of Avoca and better practices, not to the AI alone.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "Yeah. So like obviously there's a lot to that. Some of it's, uh, Avoca, some of it's like better practices there. There's a lot to that. But we went from 18 to 10, we believe that 10 is like. Kind of the number now. Yeah. And despite however much more volume we can drive, like we think that it's now frictionless"
claims.denominator: Headcount in the call centre. Period over which the change happened is NOT stated.
claims.who_measured: John Wilson, self-reported, no period given
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: and he says some of that was Avoca and some of it was better practices
claims.notes: THE MOST IMPORTANT CORRECTION IN THIS FILE. The case was briefed as '18 CSRs down to 10' as an AI result. THE OPERATOR HIMSELF REFUSES THAT ATTRIBUTION in the same breath, BEFORE he says the numbers. Any slide saying the AI cut 18 to 10 is contradicted by the source. The hedge is the first half of his own sentence, not a footnote. See c06 (a flat contradiction on the endpoint) and c07 (which shift the cut came out of).

claims.text: In the other episode, Wilson gave the call centre headcount as seven or eight, down from 18 or 19.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "So we've had two really big changes to our call center in the past year. One of them has been Avoca and one's been, like a compensation change that we've really championed. So I think like a combination of those two things, but right now we're running the leanest call center that we've ever run team wise ... but I think we're down to, seven, maybe, it might be eight, but like at one point we were at 18, 19."
claims.who_measured: Self-reported. The transcript labels this turn 'Tyson Chen' but the content is unmistakably the CUSTOMER speaking ('our call center'). THE SPEAKER LABEL IN THE SOURCE IS WRONG.
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: MUST NOT be combined with c05, the two accounts disagree
claims.notes: DIRECT CONTRADICTION WITH c05, UNRESOLVED. Same owner, same company, two episodes both January 2026, one says endpoint 10, the other seven or eight. The 18 baseline is consistent, the ENDPOINT is not. Second critical finding: 'a combination of those two things', Avoca AND a compensation change. That is the second independent instance of the operator declining to attribute the headcount drop to the AI. DO NOT put a precise endpoint on a slide. Lead with c07 instead.

claims.text: The staffing reduction came almost entirely out of overnight and weekend coverage. Wilson says daytime staffing barely moved, maybe by two people.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "now some of that's like a bunch of that was overflow and weekends. That's where we saw a ton of our dynamic changing because we had, I don't know if our daytime changed much, we might have tightened that up by two, but we had a ton of people set for 24 hours. We had them set up for weekends and we just don't have to do any of that anymore."
claims.baseline: A 24/7 staffed call centre with people set for overnight and weekend shifts
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: per the owner, on his own podcast
claims.notes: THIS IS THE REAL STORY AND IT IS BETTER THAN THE BRIEFED ONE. The win was not 'AI replaced 8 CSRs'. The win was 'we stopped paying humans to sit up all night and all weekend waiting for a phone to ring'. Far more copyable for Dana, far more honest, and it reconciles cleanly with c16. BUILD THE RECEIPTS AROUND THIS FRAMING.

claims.text: Wilson put the savings at about 30 grand a month, and did not break out how much of that was the AI.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "So being able to, for us, it was like 30 grand a month of savings. So it was a lot, that's a lot of money. so being able to just add that back in and use it for marketing or literally anything else was a win."
claims.baseline: Not stated. No before figure for the blended total.
claims.denominator: Per month, BLENDED across the answering service AND call centre staffing. NOT separated by cause anywhere.
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: a blended figure the owner did not break out, and he names a compensation change alongside the AI
claims.notes: RECOMMENDED OFF THE RECEIPTS SLIDE ENTIRELY. Verbatim and confirmed twice, but attribution fails. Nobody separates the AI from the compensation change (c06) or 'better practices' (c05). Round figure, conversational, no baseline, no period, inside a sponsor-credited episode where the vendor immediately reuses it as a selling point. The c03 plus c04 pair is a far cleaner claim about the same money.

claims.text: Wilson says two things changed in the call centre that year, Avoca and a compensation change, and credits the result to the combination.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "So we've had two really big changes to our call center in the past year. One of them has been Avoca and one's been, like a compensation change that we've really championed. So I think like a combination of those two things"
claims.who_measured: Self-reported by the operator (see c06 on the mislabelled speaker turn)
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: in the owner's own words
claims.notes: The governing caveat over c05, c06 and c08, volunteered unprompted by the operator. Genuinely useful teaching: the confound is named by the man who did the project, which is MORE credible than a clean number would have been.

claims.text: Wilson's raw booking rate, measured across all calls, is in the thirties. It was 27 when they first started tracking it.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "Like we call it raw book right now. Yeah. And like our raw book rate I think is in the thirties, which like. Is actually, that's good. Yeah. That's all calls. Yeah. It doesn't sound good, but like that's good. When we first started tracking it, it was like 27."
claims.baseline: 27, AT THE POINT THEY STARTED TRACKING. A measurement-start baseline, NOT a pre-Avoca baseline.
claims.denominator: All inbound calls, including abandoned, non-bookable and vendor calls. Wilson states it explicitly.
claims.who_measured: Wilson's own tracking, self-reported, hedged with 'I think'
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: raw rate across all calls, and 27 was where the TRACKING started, not where Avoca started
claims.notes: MATERIAL CORRECTION. The brief framed this as 27 rising into the thirties UNDER AVOCA. THE PAGE DOES NOT SUPPORT THAT CAUSAL LINK. Starting to measure is not the same event as installing the AI. The movement CANNOT be attributed to Avoca. What IS shippable is the denominator lesson: this company's honest all-calls booking rate is in the thirties and its owner considers that good. Do NOT quote the four-word fragment about all calls verbatim, renderings varied, paraphrase it.

claims.text: On the podcast, Avoca's Rafi Derringer says operators think their booking rate is 85 or 90 percent because they are not counting abandoned calls, excuse calls and vendor calls.
claims.verbatim_from_page: Rafi Derringer: "People think their booking rate is 85, 90%, but they're not factor forwards. Right. Those abandon calls. There's excuse calls, there's, there's C vendors."
claims.who_measured: Nobody. A vendor employee's characterisation of an industry-wide misconception.
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: said by Avoca's own Rafi Derringer on the podcast
claims.notes: DO NOT QUOTE VERBATIM ON A SLIDE, too garbled to read ('bookie rate', 'factor forwards' are machine-transcript artifacts of 'book rate' and 'factoring in'). PARAPHRASE ATTRIBUTIVELY WITHOUT QUOTATION MARKS. Load-bearing evidence for the denominator lesson, pairs with c10 and c12.

claims.text: On Avoca's own homepage, a testimonial credited to the Wilson Companies CEO says call quality is up from 40 percent to 95 percent, booking percentage sits at 85 percent, and they average 400 calls weekly.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "Ever since we started using Avoca in our call center, call quality is up from 40% to 95%, booking percentage sits comfortably at 85% and we're averaging 400 calls WEEKLY." Attributed to "Wilson Companies CEO & co-host of Owned and Operated Podcast"
claims.baseline: 40 percent call quality. No definition of 'call quality' is given anywhere.
claims.denominator: NOT STATED for any of the three figures.
claims.who_measured: Unstated. Presented by the vendor as a customer testimonial.
claims.date: Fetched 2026-08-15, page carries copyright 2026 Avoca AI
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: on Avoca's own marketing site
claims.notes: CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF ON LOCATION: these figures are on the HOMEPAGE, not the Wilson case study page. THE VALUABLE THING: the same man's booking rate is 85 percent on his vendor's homepage and 'in the thirties' on his own podcast, and the reason is explained by the vendor's own employee (c11). A real, teachable, verified tension. HANDLE GENEROUSLY, not as a gotcha. Both numbers are probably honest and measure different denominators.

claims.text: Avoca co-founder Tyson Chen says full AI books about 5 percent lower than the hybrid human-plus-AI setup, which is why Avoca recommends hybrid for its larger customers.
claims.verbatim_from_page: Tyson Chen: "out of our customers, it's typically what we recommend is that larger customers use hybrid because hybrid, you're just going to get a higher booking rate. Full AI the booking rate is actually significantly higher than it was before because of how human like we've gotten it ... but it's still probably around 5 percent lower overall booking rate. And so usually it's companies that are under 10 million under 5 million. There's a larger percentage that use full AI... And then for the companies that are larger than 10 million, the vast majority, we recommend, and also they do use hybrid because they want, every single percentage of that booking rate matters to them."
claims.baseline: The hybrid human-plus-AI configuration's booking rate
claims.denominator: Overall booking rate across Avoca's CUSTOMER BASE. An aggregate across customers, NOT a Wilson-specific measurement.
claims.who_measured: Avoca, from its own customer data. Hedged by the speaker with 'probably around'.
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: said by Avoca's own co-founder, about his own product
claims.notes: VERIFIED HARDEST AND IT HOLDS. Confirmed across two independent renderings, plus a third pass pulling the entire speaker turn intact to confirm 'around 5 percent lower overall booking rate' is not a summariser artifact. THE MOST VALUABLE CLAIM IN THE CASE. A vendor volunteering that his most autonomous configuration performs WORSE, and steering his biggest customers away from it, is the compounding-error lesson from AGENTIC_LITERACY delivered by the seller. Credible precisely because it costs him something. IT IS A VENDOR AGGREGATE, NOT A WILSON NUMBER, and must not be presented as Wilson's result.

claims.text: Avoca's co-founder describes onboarding as a two week process that takes about three to four hours of the call centre manager's time, starting from pre-built templates and a job type mapping.

Then you just give us access to your service Titan... you fill in the knowledge base of my questions, you give us a job type mapping, and then we take all of that, we train the system... And then the second week we'll do a final kind of testing call. and if everything works well, it'll go live. yeah, it usually just takes with your call center manager around three, three to four hours."
claims.denominator: Generic onboarding for a new customer. NOT Wilson's actual onboarding.
claims.who_measured: Avoca, describing its own standard process
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: the vendor's own description of a standard onboarding, NOT a measurement of Wilson's
claims.notes: IMPORTANT CORRECTION: this is NOT 'Wilson took two weeks to onboard'. Tyson Chen is answering co-host JACK CARR about JACK'S hypothetical company. Wilson never states his own onboarding duration. Use ONLY as 'the vendor says a standard onboarding runs about two weeks and takes three to four hours of your call centre manager's time'. The three-to-four-hours figure is the detail that makes 'bought and configured, not built' concrete.

claims.text: Wilson says it took them about 90 days to get it working well.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "I think. I feel like it took us 90 days to learn for it. To learn for sure."
claims.denominator: Time from go-live to performing well, per the operator. DOUBLE-HEDGED by the speaker with 'I think' and 'I feel like'.
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: the owner's own estimate, and he hedged it
claims.notes: The Wilson-specific half of the timeline gate, and what makes filter 5 pass alongside c14. Garbled but digits and unit stable across both renderings. The vendor's man immediately softens it in reply ('it's gonna perform at a high level from the start'), a nice small illustration of the ramp-versus-day-one tension.

claims.text: Wilson's human CSRs still pick up 90 percent of calls within seven seconds. The AI catches what they miss.
claims.verbatim_from_page: John Wilson: "I know for us one of the big priorities we were aiming at, which has been a win, is how do we get to a seven second pickup? Like a one ring pickup. Um, and we've been able to drive that. 'cause basically if my team doesn't pick it up in seven seconds, which we do 90% of our calls, it is immediately picked up. Yep. With, um, with ai."
claims.denominator: 90 percent of all calls answered by HUMANS inside seven seconds; the AI is the fallback on the remainder plus after hours
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: per the owner, on his own podcast
claims.notes: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT SCOPING FACT IN THE CASE. It reframes everything: this is NOT an AI call centre. Wilson's people still answer nine calls in ten, on the first ring. Avoca is the seven-second safety net and the night shift. Reconciles c07, explains why hybrid beats full autonomy (c13). RECOMMENDED AS THE LIMIT ON THE YOUR VERSION SLIDE. Better story too: the AI did not replace the call centre, it let them stop staffing the hours nobody wanted to work.

claims.text: Avoca detects when a caller is getting frustrated or heated from tone and emotion, and hands the call to a human.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "If the caller's getting heated, like they're getting frustrated or annoyed. Avoca knows it hears the tone, emotion, and hands the call to a real human so you can still save that call."
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: per Avoca's description of the product
claims.notes: CRITICAL HANDLING: this comes from the SPONSOR ADVERTISEMENT READ inside the episode, not the interview. Vendor marketing copy sitting inside a podcast page. Fine as a description of what the product CLAIMS to do, because the handoff design is central to the rung 4 story, but it MUST NOT be presented as John Wilson describing his own system and MUST NEVER appear as an operator quote. No measurement of how well the detection works exists anywhere.

claims.text: Avoca integrates directly with ServiceTitan at the gold tier level and can handle reschedules, check technician arrival times and look up customer information.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "It directly integrates into ServiceTitan at the gold tier level. That means it can handle reschedules, check tech, arrival times, and look up customer info."
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: per Avoca's description of the product
claims.notes: Same handling rule as c17, ad-read copy, vendor capability claim not operator testimony. THIS IS THE TOOL USE EVIDENCE FOR THE LADDER CALL. Bounded, wired-in tool use into one named system of record, textbook rung 4, and the concrete detail that lets Dana picture the thing writing into their scheduling system rather than just talking. Corroborated structurally by c14.

claims.text: Avoca markets itself as 'The AI Front Office for Service Businesses' with 'always-on agents', sells the product as an 'AI CSR', and its site footer reads 'The AI workforce for service businesses'.
claims.verbatim_from_page: "The AI Front Office for Service Businesses" / "Always-on agents that answer every call, fill every board, and keep your team focused on the work that matters." / "AI CSR" / "The AI workforce for service businesses"
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: Avoca's own words for its product
claims.notes: Raw material for the agent-washing correction, and this case supports an unusually GENEROUS version. The vendor says 'agents' and 'AI workforce', the build is rung 4, but the same vendor's co-founder says the configuration with the human in it books better (c13). NOT A DUNK. The line is roughly: they call it an AI workforce, it is really a configured workflow with a human handoff, and their own co-founder will tell you that is the version that works better.

claims.text: Avoca's inbound voice product is called Responder and its call scoring product is called Coach.
claims.verbatim_from_page: Tyson Chen: "I'll say one thing on both Responder and Coach." / homepage navigation: "CoachReal-time scoring" and "AI CSRBook jobs, 24/7"
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: per Avoca
claims.notes: Product names confirmed across two pages and two renderings, use freely. The further detail that Coach scores calls handled by HUMAN CSRs appeared in ONLY ONE rendering and is NOT confirmed to this run's standard, omit it. No measurement of Coach's effect on anything exists, so COACH MUST NOT CARRY A NUMBER.

claims.text: Both podcast episodes carry paid sponsor credits for Avoca.
claims.verbatim_from_page: Episode 173: "Special Thanks to Avoca" followed by "Looking to train your call center and improve technician performance? Avoca AI is here to help your team..." Episode 194: "At Wilson, we've saved a stupid amount of money by having AI help out with our call center, and the best tool out there that's making that happen is Avoca."
claims.label_that_must_ride_with_it: n/a, a finding about the sources
claims.notes: MATERIAL CORRECTION: the brief flagged only episode 173. BOTH episodes are sponsor-adjacent. Episode 194 contains a first-person Avoca advertisement read in John Wilson's own voice about his own company. The entire evidence base is one man, on a podcast he co-hosts, in episodes his vendor sponsors, plus that vendor's marketing site. Does not disqualify the case, but sets a HARD CEILING on how confidently any number can be stated.

killed.claim: Raw booking rate 27 percent rising into the thirties UNDER AVOCA
killed.why: The causal link is not on the page. 27 was where the TRACKING started, not where Avoca started. Nothing connects the 27 to the period before Avoca. The improvement CANNOT be attributed to the AI. Figures survive as c10 stripped of the causal claim.

killed.claim: 18 CSRs down to 10 BECAUSE OF THE AI
killed.why: Killed by the operator's own sentence preceding the numbers, 'Some of it's, uh, Avoca, some of it's like better practices there.' Numbers survive as c05 only with his caveat attached, and c06 is a flat contradiction giving seven or eight.

killed.claim: Roughly 30,000 dollars a month of savings FROM THE AI
killed.why: Demoted to c08 at low confidence. Operator names two other causes across the two episodes and nobody separates them. No baseline, no period, round number, inside a sponsor-credited episode. Recommended off the receipts slide entirely.

killed.claim: About two weeks to onboard, as WILSON'S timeline
killed.why: Misattributed. The two week figure is the vendor answering a co-host's question about the CO-HOST'S hypothetical company. Wilson never states his own onboarding duration. Survives only as c14, labelled as the vendor's standard process.

An unquantified marketing headline with no baseline, no period, no methodology, no named source. It also sits awkwardly against c16, where humans answer 90 percent within seven seconds and AI catches the remainder. NOT SHIPPABLE AT ANY CONFIDENCE LEVEL, even labelled.

killed.claim: The 85 percent and the thirties are reconciled by a denominator difference EXPLAINED IN THE PODCAST
killed.why: PARTIALLY KILLED. The ingredients are verified (c11, c10) but NOBODY on any fetched page says the 85 percent figure uses the narrower denominator. Connecting them is OUR ANALYSIS. Well supported and worth making, but it must be written as our reading, not asserted as a fact anyone stated, and it CANNOT CARRY A CLAIM ID.

killed.claim: Better Business Bureau corroboration of company size
killed.why: The constructed BBB URL resolved to a completely different business. No usable BBB record located.

killed.claim: Coach provides feedback on calls handled by human CSRs
killed.why: Appeared in only ONE rendering, fails this run's two-rendering standard. Omit or re-verify.

independent_corroboration.what_it_confirms: NOTHING. THE SINGLE BIGGEST WEAKNESS IN THE CASE. Six routes attempted: Google (CAPTCHA wall), DuckDuckGo (no results), Bing twice (swamped by Wilson Sporting Goods), a constructed BBB profile URL (unrelated business), the company's own careers page (no headcount, no revenue, no founding year), an alternate search endpoint (HTTP 422). No trade write-up, no local Akron news, no chamber or association listing, no business filing, no ranking, no non-sponsored account of this deployment. EVERY fact traces to one of exactly three parties: John Wilson speaking about his own company, the podcast he co-hosts, or his vendor's marketing site. Both episodes carry Avoca sponsor credits including a first-person ad read by Wilson himself. Even qualifying filter 1 rests on a self-authored bio. TREAT AS A SINGLE-SOURCE CASE WITH A VENDOR RELATIONSHIP RUNNING THROUGH IT.

the_limit.text: The AI is not running Wilson's call centre. His people still pick up nine calls out of ten within seven seconds. Avoca is the safety net for the tenth call and the shift nobody wanted to staff, which is exactly why the savings came out of nights and weekends rather than out of the day shift.
the_limit.why_it_is_useful_scoping_not_a_disclaime: It tells Dana exactly where this fits in their own building, which is the most actionable sentence in the case. Dana does not have to imagine handing the phones to a robot, because Wilson did not do that either. The move is far smaller and far more copyable: keep your people on the day shift, stop paying humans to sit up overnight and all weekend waiting for a phone to ring, and put the machine on the hours and the overflow. It also arms Dana with the right question for their next demo, because Avoca's own co-founder says the full-autonomy configuration books about 5 percent WORSE than the one with a human in it.

unresolved: HEADCOUNT CONTRADICTION, material. Episode 194 says 18 to 10. Episode 173 says down to seven or eight from 18 or 19. Same owner, same company, both January 2026. Starting point consistent, endpoint not. Episode numbering implies 173 predates 194 but the displayed dates say the opposite, so which statement is later cannot even be established. Any reconciliation would be invention. DO NOT PUT A PRECISE ENDPOINT ON A SLIDE. Lead with c07.

SPEAKER LABELS IN THE SOURCE TRANSCRIPTS ARE UNRELIABLE. One turn is labelled 'Tyson Chen' but is unmistakably the customer speaking. Every attribution was checked against turn content, not the label. Downstream crew must not lift a speaker label from these pages without checking the words make sense in that person's mouth.

THE SPEAKER OF THE 3,500 FIGURE IS UNCERTAIN. The transcript does not mark turns inside that block. This is exactly why the shippable claim is the BOUND, which is unambiguously Wilson's, rather than the point figure.

NO DEPLOYMENT START DATE EXISTS ON ANY PAGE. The system is live and measured, not projected (all verbs past or present, checked). But we do NOT know when it went live, so the deck cannot say how long it has been running.

NO INTEGRATION, DATA-READINESS OR CHANGE COST IS DISCLOSED ANYWHERE. Only the licence layer is on the record. The WHAT IT TOOK slide should say plainly that only the subscription cost is known, which is itself useful and honest.
verdict: SHIP, but a materially different case than the one briefed, and with the hero numbers changed. THE COST GATE SURVIVES in bounded form (c03 firm, c04 bounded). THE TIMELINE GATE SURVIVES on c15 supported by c14. ALL SEVEN QUALIFYING FILTERS HOLD. Every verb checked, nothing here is projected. THE BRIEFED STORY ('AI cut the call centre 18 to 10 and saved 30,000 a month') IS NOT SUPPORTED and the operator declines that attribution twice. THE TRUE AND BETTER STORY: Wilson's humans still answer nine calls in ten within seven seconds, the daytime desk barely moved, and what went away was paying people to sit up all night and all weekend waiting for a phone to ring. Smaller, more honest, more copyable. THE TEACHING IS THE REASON TO SHIP: rung 4 with genuine tool use into ServiceTitan and a designed handoff, the vendor sells it as 'always-on agents' and an 'AI workforce', and the correction can be generous because Avoca's own co-founder is on record that full autonomy books about 5 percent WORSE. Build on c03, c04, c07, c13, c14, c15 and c16, with c05 and c08 handled at arm's length or dropped.
